newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fish cuts agreement unlikely this year.
newsitem.headline: EU fish cuts agreement unlikely this year.

text.p: Prospects faded on Friday for agreement this year on proposed further sharp fishing cuts to save threatened stocks after European Union fisheries ministers said a complex Irish compromise needed more study.
EU officials said Britain, France and the Netherlands were among countries that called for a one-year extension of the 1992-96 fleet reduction programme.
"The Irish plan was a step forward but a lot more time is needed to sort out the technical details and to consult the fishing industry," said one official.
EU Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino made an impassioned plea to ministers to deal with the fish stocks crisis urgently and not to duck difficult decisions.
"A one-year extension is not the way to protect fish stocks and ensure the long-term future of the industry," an official quoted Bonino as telling ministers.
Ireland, the current EU president, this week suggested a 20 percent cut over three years for the most threatened stocks and greater flexibility for member states over how to reduce fishing.
"The compromise proposal gives choice to people. They can either reduce activity or reduce capacity," Irish Marine Minister Sean Barrett earlier told reporters.

The European Commission, warning that drastic action was needed to save stocks, proposed in May cuts, mainly in capacity, of up to 40 percent over six years for boats hunting the worst affected species, such as North Sea cod and herring.

British Fisheries Minister Tony Baldry reiterated that Britain would not implement any further major cuts until the problem of "quota hoppers" -- boats from one EU state which register in another to take part of its quota -- is resolved.
The issue was being dealt with by an intergovernmental conference, which is due to end next summer.

"It's a crazy situation where some 20 percent of the UK fleet is now effectively foreign owned, controlled, skippered, crewed...bringing no economic benefit to the fishing communities of the UK," Baldry told reporters.
Baldry said the new Irish text needed more study.

"There are a number of areas where further work is called for and where changes are necessary," Baldry told the meeting, noting the Irish proposal did very little to tackle industrial fishing or ending public investment in new vessels.
Portugal said the Irish plan was broadly acceptable.
"It's a good proposal," Portuguese Fisheries Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva told reporters.
But Portugal, like others, said that a 20 percent fish catch cut was too much and was against further fleet cuts.
Portugal argues it was the only country, along with Spain and Denmark, to meet capacity reduction targets set in the 1992-96 EU programme.
Spain, which has the biggest EU fishing fleet, stressed it had already done more than its share in cutting capacity and called for clarification of technical measures to curb fishing.
